content.key_idea: All studied systems detect slowness the same two-staged way: a monitored metric first crosses a warning threshold, triggering a warning action, and only reaches a fatal action either by exceeding a separate, higher fatal threshold directly, or by accumulating enough warnings (the warning count) over time.

summary: Figure 7 generalizes the slow-fault detection logic that this measurement study found repeated across systems like HBase, CockroachDB (pebble), Cassandra, HDFS and Kafka. For any monitored system metric, developers set a warning threshold (WT); crossing it triggers a warning action (blue). Independently, exceeding a separate, more severe fatal threshold (FT) directly triggers a fatal action (red) such as a log roll or service kill. A diagonal arrow shows the additional path the paper highlights: even without ever crossing the fatal threshold, if the warning count (WC) accumulates enough times, the system also escalates to a fatal action. A small 'old FT' table beside the flowchart lists concrete fatal-threshold values (20s, 10s, 2min, etc.) drawn from the real systems studied, grounding the generalized two-stage logic in the actual numbers developers picked.
